pool.prompt: Match each acronym to its full name.
pool.explanation: OTDR = Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer (fiber test instrument). MGN = Multi-Grounded Neutral (electric utility neutral wire grounded at every pole). NESC = National Electrical Safety Code (IEEE C2, aerial utility line code). LOTO = Lockout/Tagout (OSHA hazardous-energy control procedure). RUS = Rural Utilities Service (USDA funding and standards agency for rural OSP).

pool.prompt: An OSP project is federally funded through the RUS program. Which acronym represents the federal environmental review requirement that applies?
choices: MUTCD — the traffic control manual
NEPA — the National Environmental Policy Act requires environmental review of federally funded projects
NESC — the electrical safety code governs all federal utility work
LOTO — lockout/tagout is required before environmental review
pool.explanation: NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act, 42 U.S.C. Section 4321 et seq.) requires environmental review of federally funded projects, including RUS-funded fiber projects. RUS codifies its own environmental review procedures at 7 CFR Part 1970 (which replaced the former 7 CFR Part 1794 in 2016), including categorical exclusions for typical telecom/broadband construction.
pool.citation: 42 U.S.C. Section 4321 et seq. (NEPA); 7 CFR Part 1970 (RUS environmental review procedures).

pool.prompt: What is the BICSI credential most associated with inside-plant and data-center design work (covering TIA-568, TIA-569, TIA-606, and TIA-607)?
choices: RCDD (Registered Communications Distribution Designer)
CFOT (Certified Fiber Optic Technician)
CFOS/O (Certified Fiber Optic Specialist / Outside Plant)
PE (Professional Engineer)
pool.explanation: The RCDD is BICSI's primary credential for ISP and data-center design professionals, covering the telecom-spaces model and TIA cabling/administration/bonding standards. CFOT and CFOS/O are FOA (not BICSI) credentials focused on hands-on fiber technician and OSP specialist skills, not general design.
pool.citation: BICSI credentialing program scope (RCDD); FOA credentialing program scope (CFOT/CFOS).

pool.prompt: What is the key functional difference between NEC and NESC — two codes commonly confused by new OSP crews?
choices: They are the same code published under two different names

NEC (NFPA 70) governs electrical installations including cable entries into buildings and grounding; NESC (IEEE C2) governs overhead utility lines including aerial fiber attachment clearances and loading
NEC applies only to fiber; NESC applies only to copper
NESC is a voluntary guideline with no legal force; NEC is federal law
pool.explanation: NEC (National Electrical Code, NFPA 70) governs indoor/building electrical installations, including where OSP cable enters a building and how it must be grounded. NESC (National Electrical Safety Code, IEEE C2) governs outdoor overhead utility line construction — clearances, loading, attachment heights for aerial fiber. Both apply to a single fiber project, at different points along the route.
pool.citation: NFPA 70 (NEC) scope; IEEE C2 (NESC) scope — both independently verified this session (see T01.md).

pool.prompt: What does OLTS measure, and how does it differ from an OTDR test?
choices: OLTS (Optical Loss Test Set) measures end-to-end insertion loss using a light source and power meter (Tier 1); OTDR locates and characterizes individual events along the fiber (Tier 2) but doesn't need to be paired with a photodetector at the far end
OLTS and OTDR measure the exact same thing and are interchangeable
OLTS locates individual splice events; OTDR only measures total end-to-end loss
OLTS is used only for copper cable testing, never for fiber
pool.explanation: OLTS (Tier 1) gives a single end-to-end insertion loss number using a light source at one end and a power meter at the other — fast, but it doesn't tell you WHERE any loss is. OTDR (Tier 2) sends a light pulse and reads the reflected signal to locate and characterize every event (splice, bend, break, connector) along the fiber's length.

pool.prompt: What is the function of an IBT (Insulated Bonding Transformer) on a long aerial fiber run in an RUS-program (MGN) area?
choices: It amplifies the optical signal at intervals along the route
It bonds the cable messenger to the MGN while isolating the messenger from induced AC voltage, providing bonding continuity without a shock hazard from longitudinal induced voltage
It converts the fiber signal from single-mode to multi-mode
It replaces the need for a grounding electrode system entirely
pool.explanation: On long aerial runs near power lines, an IBT bonds a metallic messenger to the multi-grounded neutral (MGN) for lightning/fault protection while isolating it from dangerous induced AC voltage that can build up over long parallel runs with power lines.

pool.prompt: What does the designation "OS2" mean when it appears on a fiber cable spec, per ISO/IEC 11801?
choices: A multi-mode fiber grade used only for short indoor runs
The optical single-mode class corresponding to G.652.D SMF — the standard low-water-peak single-mode fiber for long-distance OSP and backbone deployments
A splice case classification for underground vaults
A designation for ribbon cable fiber counts above 288
pool.explanation: OS2 (ISO/IEC 11801) corresponds to G.652.C or G.652.D single-mode fiber (low/zero water-peak) — the standard for OSP trunk and feeder runs, with maximum attenuation specified at 0.4 dB/km. OS1 maps to earlier G.652.A/B specs (max 1.0 dB/km), now rare in new installations.
pool.citation: ISO/IEC 11801 OS1/OS2 fiber category mapping to ITU-T G.652 sub-categories, corroborated via multiple independent fiber-industry technical summaries (see T01.md).

pool.prompt: What is an AHJ (Authority Having Jurisdiction), and why does a single OSP project typically involve more than one?
choices: A single national regulator that oversees all aspects of an OSP project

The regulatory body or official enforcing codes in a specific location or aspect of the project — a project can have multiple AHJs (e.g., a state utility commission for NESC, a local fire marshal for NEC, the Corps of Engineers for waterway crossings)
A BICSI-issued individual credential, not an organization
An acronym specific to RUS-funded projects only, with no application elsewhere
pool.explanation: AHJ is a general regulatory-compliance term — the entity with legal authority to enforce a given code in a given jurisdiction or domain. A single fiber project can have several AHJs simultaneously, each enforcing a different applicable code (NESC, NEC, environmental, waterway crossing, etc.).
